questions.q: What does checkout-api's traffic ramp look like in the sale's first forty minutes?
options: Flat, with no change from baseline
A sharp climb and rapid HPA scale-events — from 6 replicas at baseline to 26-28 replicas by 9:40, as traffic hits 9-10x normal
A single, slow, overnight increase
Traffic actually decreases as the sale begins
questions.explain: Traffic ramps fast, then surges, triggering a series of rapid HPA scale-events — exactly the bursty pattern Lesson 8's single-origin load test never reproduced.

questions.q: What does the FinOps dashboard show by 9:45, and what does Theo report to Casey?
options: Cluster-wide CPU spiking to 99% with cost far over budget

Cluster-wide CPU averaging 58% with headroom, cost burn-down tracking on the forecasted line, and storefront's cost share scaling proportionally with traffic — Theo reports on budget, scaling as planned
The dashboard is offline and shows no data
Cost per namespace shows storefront spending nothing at all
questions.explain: Every panel built to answer 'are we spending what we expected on the capacity we have' says yes, so Theo's report to Casey is accurately reassuring based on what that dashboard shows.

questions.q: What happens at 10:15, and how serious does it look at that moment?
options: A full platform outage is declared immediately
A handful of scattered customer-support reports about slow checkouts arrive in #platform-oncall — easy to attribute to normal sale-day chatter, not yet a clear signal
The FinOps dashboard immediately shows a cost spike
Casey orders an emergency rollback
questions.explain: It's described as a 'loose thread' — a few easy-to-dismiss reports, not a flood, and not something the FinOps dashboard is showing any sign of.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say Theo is NOT making a mistake by not immediately investigating at 10:15?
options: Because customer complaints never matter

Because a few scattered complaints against a dashboard showing 58% cluster-wide CPU and an on-budget cost curve is not, by itself, a five-alarm signal — it's a loose thread, not yet connected to anything
Because Theo is not responsible for checkout-api
Because the sale is almost over by 10:15
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that this is what it realistically looks like when a healthy-looking dashboard and easy-to-dismiss reports coexist for a while before anyone connects them — not a failure of judgment.

questions.q: Why does this lesson deliberately NOT resolve the 10:15 loose thread?
options: Because the issue turns out to be nothing
Because showing what it looks like when a dashboard and scattered reports coexist unresolved for a while is the actual point — connecting them is where the next lesson goes
Because Theo quits before investigating
Because the sale is cancelled
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ends on this unease on purpose, setting up the next lesson where a separate reliability dashboard formally disagrees with the FinOps picture.
